morphology.shape: Dimorphic: mold form at room temperature (thin, branching hyphae with conidia in a "flower/daisy" arrangement), cigar-shaped yeast at body temperature
morphology.notes: The elongated, cigar-shaped budding yeast in tissue is a distinguishing microscopic feature

reproductiveStructures: Conidia arranged in a flower-like ("daisy") cluster on the mold form

habitat.naturalHabitat: Soil, decaying vegetation, sphagnum moss, and thorny plants (e.g. roses)
habitat.hostAssociation: Environmental saprophyte; introduced into skin via trauma
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Worldwide, particularly associated with gardening, landscaping, and handling of sphagnum moss or rose bushes

microscopy.stain: Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) or Gomori methenamine silver stain of tissue
microscopy.appearance: Cigar-shaped or oval budding yeast cells in tissue, often sparse and hard to find directly

culture.media: Sabouraud dextrose agar (mold form, 25-30°C); enriched media (yeast form, 37°C)
culture.growthCharacteristics: Relatively fast growing for a dimorphic fungus — days to about 2 weeks
culture.colonyMorphology: White to cream, becoming dark brown/black and wrinkled with age (mold form); smooth, cream-colored yeast colonies at 37°C

identificationClues: Classic history of a gardening/plant-related injury (rose thorn, hay, sphagnum moss) followed by nodular lesions along lymphatic channels ("sporotrichoid spread")
Thermal dimorphism with a distinctive cigar-shaped yeast form in tissue
Flower/daisy-like arrangement of conidia on the mold form under the microscope
Culture remains the diagnostic gold standard, since organisms are often sparse in tissue

diseases: Lymphocutaneous sporotrichosis ("rose gardener's disease") — nodular, ulcerating lesions spreading along lymphatics
Rare disseminated/pulmonary/osteoarticular disease, mainly in immunocompromised hosts
clinicalImportance.transmission: Traumatic inoculation of the skin by contaminated plant material (thorns, sphagnum moss, hay); rarely inhalation (pulmonary disease) or, historically in some regions, cat-associated transmission
clinicalImportance.epidemiology: An occupational risk for gardeners, farmers, florists, and forestry workers worldwide; distribution follows exposure to contaminated organic material rather than a specific climate zone
clinicalImportance.labSignificance: Culture is the diagnostic gold standard because the organisms are often too sparse in tissue for reliable direct visualization

examFacts.importantTest: Fungal culture; histopathology showing cigar-shaped yeast
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: Classic occupational/gardening exposure history with nodules spreading along lymphatic channels
